She speaks of the situation of her Daughters who are nurses in the Hospital of which he is President. They are forced to do very heavy work, including night watches, without any help from assistants. In the course of a year two have fallen seriously ill with consumption, and one has died. She has heard that their number is to be reduced to three, which would do them very grave harm, since they do not spare themselves; nor could they replace one another in case of illness. She appeals to his understanding to obtain that there be at least five.

Most Illustrious Signor Mangili,

  1. The reason I did not reply at once to your esteemed letter was, through no fault of mine, that I was not in Piacenza but at another House in Sampierdarena, and only since yesterday have I had your esteemed letter in my hands.

  2. My good Sir, I am overwhelmed to find myself so favoured and protected by Your Lordship that I assure you that, out of regard for you and at your command, I would and will place at the disposal of Your Lordship and of the distinguished Congregation every service and all that my wretched Institute can provide.1

  3. My God! Now, speaking truthfully and with all the charity I feel towards the poor sick and my wretched daughters, I must let Your Lordship know that, since the poor Nurses have to keep the night watches, no fewer than two a night, as you will find they do, it is impossible to hold out; and besides, you can see that if one of them fell ill there must be someone to replace her. In this way poor humanity will be well served,2 and the order

that now prevails will always reign, because, as you have seen, the work is tiring and the night watches are tiring; and, as you see, the Hospital has already almost taken two victims: one dead and two incurable with consumption.3 You, good protector, will say: they will give you assistants to do the menial work. No, my good Sir, because then order and good management cannot be maintained; be assured that this poor servant of yours speaks from experience: they would run into trouble and annoyance, and we into the most painful distress.

  1. It is cruel to me to hear that they are taking the management4 away from a prioress in charge of the linen room, after she has given for over a year the most active and economical service, more than if it had been her own house. And you, my protector, as an intelligent person now better acquainted with the running of the Hospital, will I hope see her conduct and how everything is managed, and with what perfection she has done her work.

  2. And to my extreme sorrow I could not bear to leave only three poor creatures here, for in doing their duty I would certainly see them succumb.5 I rely confidently on the charity I have long known to reign in Your Lordship's heart; I am sure you will take this matter up and obtain from the honourable Congregation at least the number of five.6

  3. As for the financial side, please consult the Hospital Bursar, for I am ready to make any sacrifice.7

  4. I would fly to you, but the affairs of this new House prevent me for now, all the more since we have been called to the city of Genoa to serve the sick, as I would have liked to do in your City.8

  5. If Your Lordship knew our service and the benefit it brings to humanity, I have no doubt you would have pressed the Hospital and others to increase our number, so that we could give your City the help our charity requires of us.

  6. I would not want to have bored you with this long letter, but since I cannot tell you in person I have ventured to write you everything.

10. If the most excellent Congregation wishes me to come, please be so kind as to write to me, and I shall consider myself fortunate to be able to serve it at once.

Please give my most respectful regards to your excellent wife, whose hand I greatly wish to shake, and allow me to sign myself with all esteem and respect Your Lordship's

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 The «Congregation of Charity» that administered the Hospital at Cento.

2 Poor humanity, that is, suffering humanity, the sick, will be well served, and the present order will always prevail in the hospital.

3 As he has seen for himself, the hospital has taken its victims: one has died (Sr. Daria Vagni, on 22 August 1868) and two are seriously ill with consumption.

4 They are removing the sister in charge of the linen room from her post.

5 It was indeed impossible for only three Sisters to meet the needs of the sick.

6 This number also guaranteed the Sisters' community life.

7 Let him come to an arrangement with the bursar; she was willing to reduce the nurses' pay to a minimum.

8 In Genoa she was to found a community to nurse the sick at home. She wished to be able to nurse the sick at home in Cento too.

She has heard that he wishes to offer a house of his for social works. She expresses her wish to establish there a community of Daughters of Saint Anne to nurse the sick poor at home.

Very Reverend Prior,

  1. Having been asked to come to Genoa to nurse the sick poor in their homes, and needing a dwelling, but finding none suited to this work, I remembered Your Reverence's house, which you ardently wished to make into a convent.

  2. If I could have that pleasure I would be very fortunate, and I am sure that our dear little Mother Immaculate, daughter of our Mother Saint Anne, would be greatly pleased too.

  3. If you consider me worthy of a reply, I am in this new House, the third of this Order, here at Sampierdarena, opposite the chapel of Our Lady of Graces.2

Accept my respects and believe me Your Reverence's

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 The letter dates from the first quarter of 1869, since the community, as M. Rosa says, is still lodged in Signora Bodda's house, from which it moved to the Villa Gattorno at Sampierdarena in the spring of that year. Cf. Letter 115, n. 6.

2 The rector of the chapel was Fr. Angelo Ricchini.

She asks for prayers and invites her to Piacenza with her friend.

A.M.F. A.V.E.G.Z.P.1

My friend, dear to Jesus,

  1. Two hurried lines, because I am so unwell: my poor health. I am sending you the manual of the Daughters of Saint Anne, which I am sure you will treasure. It is as beautiful as can be.2

  2. Now I want one thing from you: for charity's sake, pray for me, and that dear creature too; if you grant what I ask, I will send one of these books to your dear one as well.3 I want to know so many things, especially about that matter. I cannot explain myself in detail; you understand me as a whole.

  3. You should come here with your dear friend,4 and then we could talk more quietly. I am staying put. I really want to talk to you. Why have you not written to me again? Write to me soon and at length; you know what I want. Tell me many things.

Greet your dear friend for me and believe me

your poor friend Rosa

1 Hail, full of Grace: initials unusual in Mother Rosa's correspondence.

2 Cf. Letter 145, 3 and n. 5.

3 Her friend Rosa Parodi.

4 The friend mentioned above.

For the sister nurses to remain honourably in the hospital at Cento, the indispensable conditions must be made clear, and she is ready to do so.

Most Illustrious President,

  1. I have received your esteemed letter, with words truly worthy of a charitable father who has always shown himself generous to our Congregation.

  2. Allow me now to set out in writing to Your Lordship what this wretched little woman perceives in her mind, things that seem most right, and I am sure I shall have your approval.

  3. You know, and there is proof of it, that you love philanthropy, which leads you to sacrifice everything for humanity.

  4. So I see clearly that my nurses, who are all spirit of philanthropic charity, cannot work alongside mercenary people2 whose only aim is vile gain; so my nurses, if they can remain as they were, [will stay]; otherwise I am obliged to withdraw them; and if they stay, I am ready to give your city proof of my liveliest gratitude by offering any service of charity without any payment.

  5. Before coming I await your reply, and then I will gladly not come until I have the privilege of conferring with you.3

  6. Give my respects to your honourable wife; God willing, I look forward to shaking her hand.

Accept the sentiments of esteem and respect of one who is honoured to call herself Your Lordship's

humble Servant, Gattorno Rosa

1 President of the Congregation of Charity — Hospital of Santa Maria, Cento.

2 «Mercenary people» = interested not in the sick but in gain.

The conditions she set for the sister nurses to remain arose from the very nature of their state: they served as a community, out of charity, and not individually like lay nurses. The religious therefore had to be guaranteed the conditions proper to their particular presence, both as regards the living quarters reserved to them and in the performance of their duties. Cf. the relevant document in Arch St FSA, A. 3. 37, Mmv - 15.

3 She went to Cento on 15 April. Cf. Letter 120, 2.

Practical instructions for the Sisters who are to go to Fr. Costantino Peragallo.

\ AHI-

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. I have already written to you all about the journey, but I am truly in the depths of desolation; what I have done, my God, I do not know.1

  2. Send Santina and Domenica2 to Peragallo. Give them these reminders: to be silent, to try to win the girls' hearts, to be hard-working and good, faithful to their Rules; so they must try to do well. You, my Carolina,3 write to me at once and keep me informed of everything.

  3. Superior, give them some of the money I am sending with this letter;4 give it to Carolina, and buy them stamps and something to eat, whatever they need. Be thrifty, and tell Signora Marina5 to get some money to me. For charity's sake, silence; let them be careful to keep silence and tell her to send me the money. I do not know whether I am coming or going.6 I am

your loving Mother Rosa

1 The Mother has a great gift for expressing states of mind and situations concisely. Two days earlier she had come through the «trial» of the proceedings brought against her by the superior of the Mother House. Cf. Index II, n. 4.

2 Sr. A. Santina Solenghi and Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini.

3 Carolina Pezzoni, the headmistress. She had already decided and asked to enter the Daughters of Saint Anne and was therefore regarded as a postulant.

4 Enclosed in this letter.

5 Marina Paganelli, one of her friends. Cf. Arch St FSA Pos. Amiche.

6 See above, n. 1.

She asks for news of the sisters with Peragallo and of her son Alessandro.

A.M.F.

My good Francesca, Superior,

  1. Just two lines to ask you to go to Carolina to encourage her and at the same time get news of her: whether the teacher has gone yet,1 whether Peragallo is satisfied. Let him write and tell me whether he wants others, and when I should send them.2 Press him to take them soon.

  2. I do not know whether I shall be able to come, because today your sister left for Cento, and until Giuseppa returns; I wish no one to know of this.3

  3. Give me news of Giggino and pray that he gets better; I assure you, my dear, it is quite a sacrifice not to be able to be there to look after him.4 Patience! It is true that the Eternal Father is pleased with sacrifices more than anything else.5

  4. I would like to go on, but my head will not hold out tonight.

I am your most loving Mother, Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

God bless you

1 Whether the lay teacher has not yet left. The superior needed to visit the Sisters often, as the work was only beginning, and above all to encourage the young headmistress of the school.

2 Let him write if he wants other Sisters and, if so, press him to ask

for them soon. There were three (cf. Letters 102, n. 1 and 114, 7). The Mother wanted to form a community.

3 Sr. A. M. Luigia Camisa. Despite this Sister's reprehensible conduct (cf. Index II), the Mother gives her a concrete sign of generous forgiveness and trust by entrusting her with the post of Superior in the difficult hospital setting at Cento, in place of Sr. M. Giuseppa Troni.

4 Her son Alessandro was then 14 and had been ill on and off since January.

5 Inasmuch as they are expressions of love and fidelity.

She teaches the young woman to advance in the way of charity, following Jesus.

A.M.F.

My dear little Daughter Carolina,

Blessed be our holy Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate.1

  1. I received your dear letter, which I had so longed for. It reached me at 11 in the morning. My dear, what good news you give me; yes, the Lord will love his Carolina more and more, he will pour arrows of love into her heart.

  2. Dear Jesus,2 burn her, consume her entirely with divine fire. Oh! Dear Spouse of the beloved Love! How dear I find this name given to a daughter of mine! Jesus, beloved of frank and good souls, you who are truth and life, you who love those who bear truth on their lips, make my Carolina a true dove3 and your model in speech.

  3. I hear, my dear, all you tell me, and I see the tribulations you have suffered; so, courage! Saint Anne, our Mother, will reward you. Be sure that this is certain for those who suffer; one day you will see your sorrows turned into so many gems, your sufferings into jubilation and consolation.4 Ah, my dear, believe me, I am with you in thought, and if I could fly, how often I would have fluttered over San Nicolò!5

  4. I am preparing the teacher to come and replace you, and others too;6 but what can I do? the long thorns in this house, my God! give me a fountain of patience! Carolina, have others pray, and pray yourself, for this poor Mother of yours.

  5. I cannot understand how Peragallo came to put you at table with ladies,7 but I hope you are now on your own, for I urged it on him so strongly: you must be on your own, entirely on your own. But he is so good that little by little he will arrange everything for you as your Rules require. Write to me at once: how is it going with the teacher? Do not be distressed, for the holy Mother will make everything turn out well and will accept her Carolina's desire to be exact in keeping her holy Rules.

  6. My dear daughter, for charity's sake, trample on human respect and flee such thoughts. Look, I will teach you what to do when you see certain good souls failing in certain duties of piety. This is how it is done: you at once occupy your mind with this thought: poor things, they are not thinking of it; I will quickly make the sign of the cross8 myself; and so it will remind them that they forgot to make this Christian gesture; and so on. So it is in everything. My dear, try to do as this wretch teaches you.

  7. I would stay much longer, and gladly, if I had a moment; but, dear Jesus, I am so overwhelmed that I truly have not a minute's breathing space to do what I would like. My health is still poor and I am always struggling with stomach pain.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you and the other two Daughters of Saint Anne too. Let them pray for me.

I am your most loving Mother, Sr. A. M. Rosa Gattorno

8. You did well in all you did and said. Be at peace and of good heart

1 This is the first time we find in the greeting of a letter the aspiration to Saint Anne prescribed in the 1869 Rules.

2 This shift of person in the dialogue is typical of the Mother's letters: she turns from her correspondent to address directly another person, God, whose presence she lives and with whom she relates spontaneously and with spiritual ardour. Hence the invocations or fervent prayers, apt to the persons and circumstances, that punctuate her writing.

3 A true dove. Simplicity is one of the characteristic virtues of the holy Mother's Family. The 1869 Rule, which the Foundress was instilling in her Daughters, says: «let everything in you be light», and calls it «dovelike simplicity» (Rule 1869, Ch. 1).

4 Pauline thought shines through these and similar expressions: «this momentary light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison» (2 Cor 4:17).

5 Salita San Nicolò: the street of the «Retreat» founded by Fr. Peragallo in the Convent of San Nicolò, where the Sisters worked.

6 Come and replace you, and other Sisters.

7 In the work, along with the girls, Fr. Peragallo had also taken in some elderly ladies (cf. Carolina Pezzoni's letter of 3 April 1869, Arch St FSA, D. 1).

8 I will make the sign of the cross (which the other carelessly neglected), which for a Christian is a profession of faith.

She thanks her for the news and asks for more. She will send the money soon.

A.M.F.

My dear Superior,

  1. I have just received your letter and am answering from bed. Thank you for the news you give so truthfully. Do you know, dear, what Angiolina does? She puts the old stamps on all the letters; whoever receives them, ourselves included, gets the old stamp and so has to pay more.1

  2. I am sorry to hear you have no money. I am sending you a money order for 30 francs at once.2

  3. I did not quite understand your letter where you tell me about the schools, Santina and Peragallo. Write and tell me at once, and then I will send you another [sister], straight away with Dominichina.3

  4. I can only clasp you in the Heart of Jesus, that you may soon be consumed by his divine love.4 I can do no more, but I hope to get up soon and write to you at length, and to Carolina too.

Goodbye! Greet all the Daughters of Saint Anne for me; may the Lord bless them, and pour out a most abundant one5 upon you.

And I am for ever your most loving Mother6

1 Angiolina, Fr. Angelo Ricchini's housekeeper. Cf. Letter 103, n. 6.

2 The community needed financial support. Poor, yes, but the Sisters and the girls, now quite numerous (17), must not lack necessities. Cf. Sr. A. Francesca Camisa's letter of 23 April 1869, Arch St FSA, F. 3. 24.

3 Domenica Pastorini, who would take the name Sr. A. Nazzarena.

4 She could give her no other sign and proof of affection, nor any other wish. The essential thing, the one purpose of life, is to let oneself be taken and consumed by the love of Jesus.

5 Blessing.

6 This letter is addressed: Villa Gattorno - Sampierdarena.

She gives news of her health and urges her to take care of herself.

A.M.F.

Read these lines to the Daughters1

My dear Superior,

Always remember these words: let Truth be your treasure,

always.

Blessed be our Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate.

  1. Thank you for the news you give me. I hope you have received the money order.2 I am up, but I feel very ill. I have pains everywhere, one might say. Now, my dear, I close because I can do no more,3 but tomorrow, if I am up, I will write again.

  2. I am extremely sorry about your health. For charity's sake, take care of yourself, try to eat something, and if you cannot, do not go out4 and do not go to Genoa. If you see Firpo,5 give him my regards. Thank you for all you have done for me.6 Soon, I hope, I will thank you in person.

Goodbye! I am your most loving

Mother Rosa

1 She refers to the letter she encloses for the Daughters, given below.

2 She had sent her 30 francs five days earlier.

3 The Mother kept no secrets about her health from Francesca.

4 Do not go out.

5 Fr. Giuseppe Firpo, M. Rosa's former spiritual director.

6 All you have done. She had not only nursed her with love and devotion during her serious illness (cf. Letter 85, 6), tirelessly caring for her day and night; she helped her in God's Work, looked after Alessandro and loved him like a son.

She spends what health the Lord grants her on the House of Saint Anne. She feels she has done far too little so far.

A.M.F.

Dear Daughters of Saint Anne,

God bless you, and may truth always remain on your lips, and simplicity in your hearts.1

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate.

  1. I thank you infinitely for the prayers you offer for my health; and believe me, when the Lord gives me a little, I spend it at once for the good of the House of Saint Anne, like the Eternal Father's poor donkey, which, when it feels a little strength, knows nothing else but to carry the load its God puts on its shoulders; but to my regret, so far I have carried little in the past, nothing now, and in future I shall be good for nothing more than dragging this corpse about.2

  2. What wages will I get? An abyss of punishment for having lived so badly. My Jesus will say to me: how often I loaded you, and you threw off the load and ruined everything, you who never did anything for me, being lazy to excess.3

  3. Dear Daughters of Saint Anne, your Mother and mine — though I am unworthy to be called so — yet Daughters! You know well that [I am] proud and full of presumption:4 that is what I am. I will soon be with you. I hope to find those dear creatures Saint Anne desires, keeping the holy Rules from the moment they open their eyes in the morning until evening, when sleep overtakes them.

4. Goodbye! Speak little and pray much. You will be glad of it, not only on the day of judgement but now as well, for in silence the soul can converse with Jesus, always finds her Spouse and enjoys union with him.

I am your very poor Mother, Sr. A. M. Rosa

1 A virtue dear to the Mother, who rejoiced to see her Daughters adorned with it. She suffered, and her heart filled with bitterness, when she found «duplicity» and «falsehood».

2 The main body of the letter unfolds with realism and awareness of her limits, tinged with pessimism, the effect of debilitating physical prostration: I feel very ill... I have pain everywhere... I can do no more. But it is realism read with humility and faith. On her journey with God she spends all she receives to please the Eternal Father.

3 What wages will I get? An abyss of punishment. Comparing what she has received with what she has given him, she feels lacking and lazy. Her small goodness is infinitely far from his infinite goodness.

4 Proud and full of presumption. This is the language of humility. God's greatness and purity light up every hidden corner of her inner world. To lower oneself thus is to rise. Cf. Ps 130.

She thanks her for her visit with her friend.

Dear friend,

God bless you, my sweet friend, dear to Jesus

Blessed be Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. How dear that day was to me! I thank you for it and hope you will soon grant me another; and not only that, I want you to stay with me for at least two or three days. That dear creature too.1

  2. I have been so ill, and now I have been getting up for two days, and soon I will be at Sampierdarena. I am sending you some «capino» peaches2 of the Holy Father Pius IX. Give a few to those good souls.3 I close, because in a minute it is time for chapel.4

Goodbye. Pray hard for one who calls herself yours in the heart of Saint Anne.

Your most affectionate Friend, Sr. Anna Maria Rosa

1 She and her friend Rosa Parodi had spent a whole day at the Mother House.

2 A variety of peach.

3 Rosa's family.

4 In a few moments it will be time to go to the chapel to pray.

She is about to go to Cento. She asks her to have Alessandro treated.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

  1. I have received your two letters, but you say nothing about having received the money order.

  2. In greater haste than ever: I got up a few moments ago and tomorrow I leave for Cento. Dear Francesca, silence, for charity's sake.2 This poor Mother of yours hopes the Lord will help her, for she has neither strength nor life.3

  3. My dear, I will enclose two lines for Signora Maddalena, the one who treated me, and I want you to take them to her at once and ask her to treat my Giggino and to send all the doctors away, for charity's sake.4

  4. Goodbye, dear. I will write to you from Cento, but on Saturday I will be back here. Write to me here in Piacenza, so that when I arrive I find letters from you.

Goodbye; I am your most loving Mother Rosa

1 This letter, enclosed in the following one, is from the same day, as its content shows.

2 Silence: an indispensable rule of prudence. Why spread news that might cause alarm, since she hoped, as on other occasions, to smooth out the difficulties?

3 To undertake a journey in such poor health, when travelling made her suffer so much, was an act of courage; her constant pressing on was trust in the Father.

4 Having experienced the effectiveness of «natural» remedies herself, she wanted them used for Alessandro, who was not recovering. He had trouble with one leg, and radical surgery was feared. Cf. Alessandro's letters, Arch St FSA, A. 1.6.

She has to go to Cento. On her return she will go to Genoa.

A.M.F.

My dear, beloved little daughter,

  1. I received your dear letter today and at once take to heart the sweet words you use towards this most unworthy mother of yours. They refreshed me amid so many tribulations. My God! Do, do with this donkey of yours whatever you will! My dear, when that blessed hand of the Eternal Father strikes us, ah, how sweet are its blows! Yes, my dear, I would do nothing but kiss it and clasp it.1

  2. I would like to tell you so many things, but I am overwhelmed with work; I have been up for only three days, and tomorrow I go to Cento. For charity's sake, say nothing. I have written it to the Superior2 too, but in secret; only you two know. Silence, for charity's sake; today is Wednesday and I leave on Thursday, tomorrow. On Saturday I will be back and I hope next week to be in your arms.

Do not hold it against me3 that I write so little, but I really cannot stay any longer. Goodbye;

I am your most loving Mother, who clasps you in the heart of Saint Anne to enclose you there for eternity.4

Goodbye

1 Expressions of filial abandonment to the Father's will in the sad circumstances of those days, including the bad news from Cento.

2 Sr. A. Francesca Camisa.

1 Do not blame me if I write so little.

4 A mother entrusting to Mother Saint Anne this young woman, still a postulant, yet already grown in spirit.

She is back from Cento. In a few days she will be at Sampierdarena.

A.M.F.

My Caterina,

  1. Two hurried lines. In two days I shall be at Sampierdarena. I will let you know at once. What things you will hear, my God! My dear.1

  2. I came back from Cento only two days ago. You certainly cannot imagine how well the Sisters are placed there now. You will hear.

I am your most loving Mother Rosa2

1 A few lines, but what affection and familiar confidence in keeping her dear daughter, still at home, informed about God's Work! The Mother already feels she is a Daughter of Saint Anne.

2 A little letter from Carlotta to her dear friend Caterina follows. Dear Caterina!

I received your dear letter, thank you infinitely, I never forget you, I remember you.

I write soon, I pray always, dear Jesus blesses you always, gives you many graces. I love very very much friendship Caterina innocent like a Guardian Angel, I will write to you at length.

Goodbye, dear Nina, I kiss you, greetings to your sister Emilia, and I am your

most loving sister Carlotta Custo

She has sent a sack of maize flour, which must be collected from the station. She is short of money and in debt.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter and Superior: let truth be your treasure

  1. I received your letter. All the news you give me was very welcome, except that about Giggino. How sorry I am at his obstinacy! He would certainly get better. Patience!1

  2. Yesterday, the 20th, I sent you a sack of ground maize flour. Go to Fr. Ricchini and ask him to have it collected by that railway man he mentioned, so as not to pay. In this way you will save three francs.2

  3. My dear, I had a lot, but now, with the bills I had to pay that had been prepared for me,3 I am still left with a debt of 500 francs. My dear, it is pitiful.4 I would have come already, but I cannot because of a matter I must finish.

  4. I hope the Lord will soon settle everything,5 and I will be with you. I would like to know whether Fr. Angelo6 received the samples of rosaries and holy pictures, and my letter. Ask him whether he is angry, since he deprives me of his news. Two lines I know I do not deserve, but even to the unworthy one can write a word. Give him my particular regards, and pray; for although I am here, I have also thought of a Priest,7 provided he is willing to accept. I add nothing more, for I shall soon be with you, perhaps before the end of the week, if I finish this business.

Goodbye. I am your most loving Mother

5. P.S. Greet all my dear Daughters, and I am yours. The Lord bless you8

A few lines from Carlotta follow. (Transcribed below in note 8.)

1 The boy would not submit to the remedies his mother recommended. Cf. Letter 119, 3.

2 Having the goods collected by the railway employee Fr. Ricchini suggested is a way of saving. There is not only poverty but debt.

3 Apparecchiato: prepared.

4 It is pitiful. A large debt, rising expenses, no income. Anyone who truly grasps this bankrupt financial picture is moved to compassion and pity.

5 For the debt and everything else she trusts in the Lord's timely intervention: «he will soon settle everything».

6 Fr. Angelo Ricchini.

7 She was looking for a priest to act as chaplain of the house, to ensure daily Mass for the community.

8 Dearest Sister, Superior of Jesus,

I never received your letter. Angry, very sorry. I do not want to go to Genoa and accompany [in the company] of dear Father [Tornatore]. I hug you, and I am your

Carlotta Custo

An exhortation to prayer, observance of the Rules and obedience.

A.M.F.

My dear little daughter,

  1. I arrived at a quarter past eleven after a beautiful journey, all the work of your prayers; but at a village just before Piacenza I got a very bad headache, and so as soon as I reached home I felt ill. I put it down to weakness, and since I was not in pain I was able to pray a great deal; but I hope it will be nothing much. It is now five past three. I am still suffering and feel ill; but, as you see, I am writing to you in my own hand.

  2. Pray, pray all of you, my beloved ones. Remember what I told you on the last evening I had the privilege of being with you. Obey, if you want to be saints, and God grant that there may soon be in you that holy, exact observance of Chapter II of our holy Rules.1

  3. Yes, my little daughters, ready for anything. If your mother Delegate set you to clean the latrines for the whole of your life, believe me, if you do it in a true spirit of obedience, I assure you that you will become holy in that office too, just like those in more important posts which seem more likely to make one holy.2 No, my little daughters, be sure that all holiness lies in obedience.3

  4. I will not write more, because my head aches and I feel unwell.4

Goodbye. May your Rules be your whole treasure, and may the Lord's blessing fill you with every good.

I am your loving, very poor Mother Rosa

Delegate, God bless you in particular and make you holy

1 Prayer, obedience, observance. The Mother wants to build Daughters of Saint Anne on solid foundations of holiness.

Prayer: the constant activity of living in intimate communion with God

(cf. Letter 16, 3).

Obedience: unconditional submission of the will to God, a sure guarantee of

holiness.

Observance: assimilating the spirit of the Institute through the characteristic virtues and the

actions by which that spirit is acquired, perfected and spread (cf. Rule 1869,

Ch. 2).

2 Obedience in everything, promptly. It is not the more or less important offices that give life its value but the spirit of obedience.

3 All holiness, because obedience continues the obedience of Christ, into which it is grafted.

4 A very human conclusion.
She reassures and encourages her. She will visit her soon.

She encloses a letter for Caterina Rapallino and asks her to deliver it in person. Various news.

A.M.F.

Dear little daughter, my Superior

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate.

  1. Sr. Luigia arrived safely.1 How is Carolina? If she is no better, take her to have a little decoction.2 Do me the kindness of going to Caterina and taking her these two lines, which are a reply to the letter she wrote me. For charity's sake, let her mother not notice, nor anyone.3 You could try going to the Carmine very early, as she will be there, and then you can speak to her and give her the letter secretly, but at once, for charity's sake.

  2. Do not forget to note down the ten francs given to Signora Morando for the flour. You will have understood why Sr. A. M. Luigia was withdrawn: for fear of what you know.4 How is the work going? Here I found a real uproar. Let us hope that with the Lord's help everything will be settled.

  3. My health is poor. I am very swollen and fear I shall have to take to my bed, because after carrying its load the donkey lies down. So when I work, I end up lying down.5

  4. My dear, I would write more, but it must be past midnight, so I really feel the need to go to bed. I will soon be with you. If anything happens to you, write to me at once. Yesterday I sent the paper to the Superior,6 and I hope he will soon come to hear your confessions. If you see him, give him my regards, and Signora Bodda too. How is she? Try to go there,7 even though it is a sacrifice.

Goodbye, my daughter. The Lord bless you and your Daughters; greet them and ask them to pray for me.

And I am your most loving and very poor Mother

Sr. A. M. Rosa

1 After the community of the Daughters of Saint Anne, of which she was superior, withdrew from the hospital at Cento, Maria Luigia Camisa was sent by Mother Rosa to the Sampierdarena community in the belief that the Superior Francesca, Luigia's sister, could help her reconsider her religious life. Later, realising that she was causing problems for the community and for her sister, Mother Rosa thought it best, in agreement with Father Tornatore, to call her back to herself in Piacenza. Cf. Letter 126, n. 1.

2 Cf. Letter 88, n. 10.

3 Her parents persisted in refusing their consent to her becoming a religious.

4 You will have understood. Just a hint, with discretion and delicacy.

5 Just as the donkey throws itself down after the hard work of carrying, so she... A fine irony about her own weakness and limits.

6 The paper: the authorisation for Father Francesco Dassano, Superior of the Lazarist Fathers, to hear the Sisters' confessions.

7 To the church of the Carmine, to deliver the letter.

She explains why her sister has been transferred, encourages her and urges her to treasure her present suffering.

A.M.F.

My dear Superior,

  1. Just two lines, because it is very late and I am not well. May the will of my God be done for ever.

  2. I hope you understood the telegram properly and the reason that obliged us to remove Sr. Luigia, since there was a danger of serious trouble; I am sure I have relieved you of a very heavy and nasty burden to carry.1

  3. Let us pray to God, my dear daughter, for this creature, that she may mend her ways, and may God deliver us from so ugly a monster.2 My Francesca, let us make use of these precious moments to lay up some savings for eternal life; this is the precious moment whose value we shall one day recognise, and then we shall weep for having neglected such precious moments.3

  4. Goodbye, my dear; courage on the way to Calvary, if you want to be crucified with your Beloved and die with him on the delightful bed of the Cross.4

Goodbye, for I cannot go on. God bless you, and believe me

your very poor Mother, Sr. Anna Maria Rosa

1 Reasons of prudence, to avoid giving bad example outside as well as within the community; and also to relieve the superior of a «very heavy

and nasty» burden. This was her own sister, loved but lacking in religious spirit — as had been proved. Her presence therefore created an extremely delicate and difficult situation in the community.

2 Let us pray, for her and for ourselves: prayer, because God's intervention can change her heart and keep us far from the monster of infidelity and falsehood.

3 With psychological finesse the Mother urges Francesca not to be overcome by feelings, so as not to lose the value of that suffering which, accepted with love, would earn her an increase of her treasure in heaven (cf. Mt 6:20).

Let us try to use these precious moments to lay up a little wealth for eternal life; this is precisely the precious moment whose true value we shall one day recognise, and then we shall weep for having failed to make such important moments bear fruit.

4 It is Saint Paul's goal: «I have been crucified with Christ» (Gal 2:20), expressed with the accents of Rosa's unmistakable passion: to die with him on the delightful bed of the Cross.

A warning not to use any title when addressing letters to her. Advice on how to behave towards a person who is to visit the work.

A.M.F.

Francesca, my dear Superior,

  1. First of all, if you do not want me to send your letters back, change the address on the envelope.1 This is the address you must put: To Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno. If you change a single word, I will send them back and not write to you again, because, my dear, I have enough knives piercing me, and this is a most repugnant word to me, that is, words that announce the pure road to hell. I never was anything and I am nothing.2 Out of your goodness you give me the name of Mother, though I do not deserve it.

  2. Now to the telegram.3 I did not answer it because I had been informed of everything; rest assured, all will go well. If they have not yet come, I urge you to receive them with all cordiality and good manners, offering him water or wine to refresh himself, and then humbly commend to him the chapel and the house, asking him to be a Father and benefactor to us in granting permissions, and saying that we hope for everything from him.4 My regards; I will come soon, and then we will go and do our duty,5 finding out the most convenient time for him to receive us, and where, at home or at the Curia.

  3. As for that lady: we never take ladies as boarders. To become a nun one must... tell her very clearly all the sacrifices involved: the austerity of life, poor food, in short the perfect life of community, the dowry, nursing the sick.6 As for the rest, I will be with you in a few days; I hope on Monday, on Wednesday at the latest.7

Be cheerful and greet everyone for me. I will look for the thread,8 and if there is any, I will bring it.

Goodbye. The Lord bless you, and I am

your most loving Mother. Greet everyone for me

1 Sr. A. Francesca had used the title Foundress of the Daughters of Saint Anne in the address.

2 If you do: if you change even one word of what I said, I will send them back... because I have enough knives: I have enough causes of acute suffering, and this word, foundress, is repugnant to me; it is the language of vainglory and pride, the expression of the inner attitude that leads to hell. «I never was anything»: a Genoese idiom = I always was and always am nothing.

3 The superior had sent her an urgent telegram about the visit of an important figure from the Curia of Genoa, the Vicar General Chiarella. She had already been told of the same visit by Father Francesco Dassano, superior of the Lazarists, in a letter of 31.5.1869.

4 Minutely precise advice on receiving a distinguished guest who was not well disposed towards the Daughters of Saint Anne and their work in Sampierdarena, no doubt because he had been misinformed about them. Cf. Letter 131.

5 We will do our duty: we will return the visit, so let her make an appointment.

6 A succinct description of the life of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

7 Al più lungo: at the latest. Embroidery thread.

She announces that she will come to Sampierdarena. The schools inspector should be told so that he can visit them during the week.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter and Superior,

  1. As I cannot come next Tuesday, having a great deal to do with the looms, I have had to put it off until Tuesday the 15th.

  2. Have the schools inspector told, so that he can come during the week. Then go to the Superior1 and tell him that I thank him and have received his letter, but that I am not replying because on Tuesday I shall be in Sampierdarena and will bring him the paper of the privileges.2 I will do my duty in person; tell the household so.3

  3. I hope the Lord has healed you, and our dear teacher Carolina too.4 Take care of yourself. I would like to stay longer, but time does not allow it. I had to write thiss in several sittings.

Goodbye. The Lord bless you; I am your poor Mother

4. P.S. One more moment at my disposal.

My dear Daughters, I assure you that this poor mother of yours has nothing in mind but your holiness and, unworthy as she is, never ceases to raise prayers to the Most High for your spiritual and temporal welfare.

5. I must urge you — something always on my mind6 — to try to keep among yourselves that holy equality of affection; and, further,

when something happens in the house, try to keep silent and not lose your composure,7 but bring everything calmly to the feet of Jesus crucified.

6. He will put everything right and give you peace and comfort in the adversities of this wretched life. Often remember why you became religious. Answer: to become a saint; so, if that is what you want, often read the book you carry in your pocket8 and try to imprint it on your heart and mind so as to observe exactly all it contains, and God will help you put it into practice, and by this means you will become saints.

Goodbye

1 The Superior: cf. Letter 125, n. 6.

2 Cf. Letter 97, n. 3.

3 To the sisters and the people of the house.

4 Carolina Pezzoni was tenderly loved by both.

5 Writing this letter in several sittings.

6 Which is continually in her thoughts.

7 Try to keep silence and not lose your peace.

8 The book of the Rules, of which each had a copy; it was printed in pocket format.

She is to go to Fr. Angelo to clear up a misunderstanding about accepting girls.

A.M.F.

My Superior,

  1. I have just received your dear letter, together with Fr. Angelo's.1 I reply in haste so that you can go to that Reverend gentleman. Tell him in person: «Reverend Father, the Mother wishes you to know that she has never refused to accept girls, and every time you have presented any she has always taken them in; so do not fail to send those you recommend». Let him see that they have at least a mattress,2 and the camp beds will be paid for.

  2. Get the bill from him and pay it if you can; if not, I will pay it on Tuesday. Do this at once,3 even though you have already written to him; it does not matter.

  3. So go and tell him: «the Mother has never refused those you recommended whenever you sent them; on the contrary, she herself told you to send them. I only ask that they have the little mattress, and then send them all». As for the camp beds, do as I wrote above. On Tuesday or Monday at 6 I will be with you.4

Goodbye. I am

your most loving Mother Rosa

1 The girls were usually presented by their parish priest with a certificate of good conduct and genuine poverty. Cf. Arch FSA. The Fr. Angelo in question is the parish priest of the church of the «Rimedio», which Rosa Gattorno attended for Eucharistic adoration when she was a widow (Fiocchi, op. cit. I, p. 76. Cf. Letters 207, 5 and 244, 2).

2 At least the mattress, given the financial straits of the house.

3 At once. She urges and repeats her instructions, for the two reasons given above.

4 Tuesday, 15 June.

She tells her of her forthcoming arrival.

A.M.F.

Dear Carolina,

  1. Cheer up, dear Carolina: on Monday I will be with you, and then I will take you to the house in Piacenza to rest.

  2. Bear a little more suffering for the Lord,2 for that good [Father] repays everything a hundredfold.

  3. I will not write at length, because I will tell my dear Carolina everything in person.

Goodbye. I am

your most loving Mother Rosa

1 The Mother had been at Sampierdarena since Tuesday the 15th of that month and would go to Genoa on the following Monday, the 21st. This letter was therefore written between the 15th and the 19th.

2 A little more suffering. Life was hard because of the heavy work and responsibility (cf. Pezzoni's letters, Arch St FSA, D. 1).

How Signora Morando is to speak to the Vicar, who is ill disposed towards the Sisters and their work.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. Here I am at last spending a little time with my Franceschina, though my health is very bad.1

  2. My daughter, how are things going in that house? Courage, for carrying the cross requires strength, courage and generosity. I would like to know something about Caterina, but how? Let us leave everything and come, as briefly as possible,3 to the most important business of this house. Tell Signora Morando4 to go to the Curia to see the Vicar Chiarella. She may tell him whatever she likes, but in particular5 she must not forget what he told her in confession about me, that she should try to come and listen to me and get me to talk and then report it to him, and about the nuns too. And then everything; let her forget nothing.

  3. Let her tell him too6 that it was his saying this, when he had known me since I was a child, that made her suspicious. Then let her commend herself to Saint Anne7 and say everything for the glory of God and of our glorious Mother Saint Anne.

  4. Let her tell him too8 that there are a great many witnesses to his way of proceeding and that, if he wishes, she will bring them to him; and that what he wants, if he could manage to discredit us, is for the benefactors to withdraw. But he will do it all in vain,9 together with his devout ladies.

  5. Goodbye, my dear daughter. I will write to you soon and, if my health allows, at length. Burn this letter. For charity's sake, do not let anyone have it in their hands, not even Signora Morando. Let her hear everything that concerns her and then burn it.

Goodbye. I am

your most loving poor Mother Rosa

1 Gramissima: in very poor condition.

2 Caterina Rapallino, who was still at home with her family.

3 As briefly as possible: concisely.

4 Tell Signora Morando. She prefers the Superior, rather than herself, to deal with the matter with the lady.

5 In particular. This is where the plot begins, and it is worth being precise. In confession the Vicar Andrea Chiarella had spoken to her about the Mother and suggested that she visit her, get her to talk and pay attention to what she said, and then report her words and those of the sisters to him.

6 Tell him everything... tell him too. Another key point. He was gathering information about the Mother although he had known her since childhood. This had made the lady suspicious.

7 It is a task that requires the courage of truth. Let the lady commend herself to Saint Anne and be convinced that all her words aim at the glory of God and of Saint Anne.

8 Tell him too. Finally the proof, the facts. She could bring before him many witnesses ready to testify about his conduct. His intentions are now public knowledge: if he could, he would discredit the sisters' work to the point of driving all their benefactors away.

9 He will do it all in vain together with his devout ladies. Note the prophetic force of the expression: she foresees the matter dragging on.

She urges courage and trust in God, and answers various questions.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior, my Daughter,

Blessed be our holy Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Yesterday I received your letter of this month. I hear everything and assure you that this poor Mother of yours shares your afflictions. But I would like1 you to imitate me in courage and trust in God, the sole object of our actions, for we do everything for him alone and want our wages from him alone, never from men.

  2. My dear, I am writing to you on a bench by the looms, sitting almost on the floor, with their noise deafening me.2 How did it go with the girl Fr. Antonio recommended? Has she come back?3 Write me something.

  3. Now I will answer all you want to know. First: everything you did is fine. Second, as for the little girl whose father came, let us pray the Lord to move that father's heart to acknowledge her, and seek nothing else.4 If the Reverend sends any more, accept them.5 As for the Curate, I will speak with the Father and hear what he says. I will write and tell you what to do.

  4. This evening I am sending you a sack of maize flour; keep an eye out for it; I am addressing it to the railway man.6 As for money, I would be in favour of writing to Signor Montano, and so is the Father.7 I will write to you this evening.

Goodbye for now; I clasp you in the heart of Saint Anne, our Mother, and I am

your poor Mother Rosa

God bless you; of all of you I am the most wretched Daughter of Saint Anne, our Mother

5. P.S. On Tuesday you will have a visit from the Secretary.8 Be sure to have someone with you, give him a warm welcome and offer him9 lunch or refreshments. Mamma10 sends greetings and asks you to look after her chicks. Are they well?

1 She is always in tune with her daughter Francesca, worried about running the house and about poverty; she understands her and wants her to be her «imitator»... These expressions, with a bold beat of the wings, raise one to the horizon of everything and only for God.

2 They stupefy me with their deafening noise. There were more than thirty of them!

3 Fr. Antonio Accinelli. Cf. Francesca Camisa's letter of 10 June 1869.

4 The hardness of heart of this earthly father, who had taken his daughter away from a safe place, could only be melted by the tenderness of the heavenly Father; prayer must obtain that he behave towards his daughter as a true father, acknowledging her legally.

5 If the Reverend, Fr. Angelo Ricchini, sends other girls, accept them.

6 The railway employee. Cf. Letter 122, n. 2.

7 As for money, I would be in favour of writing to Signor Montano; Father Tornatore thinks the same. Niccolò Montano, a man of standing, was a member of the Municipal Council and later became president of the new Hospital at Sampierdarena. He was a benefactor of the community. Cf. Arch St FSA, posiz. Fondaz. Sampierdarena.

8 The secretary of the Municipality, Signor Giuseppe Antonio Parodi, another benefactor.

9 Esibirai: you will offer him lunch...

10 Mamma Adelaide, on a visit to Piacenza, had entrusted her chicks to her.

Advice on how to treat the girls. Her sister M. Luigia has decided to leave the Institute. Exhortations and advice.

A.M.F.

My dear little daughter,

  1. I received your letter today. My God, do with us what you will! Isn't that so, my dear Franceschina?1 I reply to yours. I feel your afflictions more than ever and hasten at once to find a way to relieve at least some of them.

  2. Listen: go to mamma and ask her to have Signora Pellina see whether she has a room to lodge a priest, but cheaply, because we are looking into2 whether we can take a priest here; then, apart from lodging, you will provide his meals and he will be with you all day.3

  3. Then, do not give the girls polenta any more. Try to give them bread; take them at once for an outing to the Guardia, on a weekday; or else to San Cipriano, because I fear they would get too tired. Give them some salami,4 which I will send you tomorrow, to be held at the station, together with a piece of lard; and in two or three days I will send you a sack of white flour and 50 francs. Tomorrow evening, with two more lines from me,5 and as I get money I will send it to you. Dear Francesca, I need not tell you how poor we are; you know.

  4. Now let us come to your sister.6 First: every individual is master of her own actions; so know that your sister herself found somewhere else to go. My dear, how many lies!7 For charity's sake, remember well what this poor Mother of yours has told you and tells you: never tell lies; let truth always be on your lips, and you will live secure in the heart of Saint Anne, our Mother.

  5. So I leave you, my dear, [to think] what I did for this

creature.8 My God, have mercy and fill her with graces.9

  1. As for you, do not think about it, because never, never again, for it is certain that you do not want to change Institute. So be cheerful, for you will always live in the heart of our Mother Saint Anne, and be in the arms of this unworthy servant of hers.10

  2. Now, do you know what she wants? All her trousseau, and she will not hear reason.11 In three years you know how many expenses and clothes there have been. Besides, I know that your mother had not sent you everything; so it would be good for you to write to your father asking that the linen goods and table linen be kept for you. And then, my dear, I leave it to you to look after your own interests.

  3. I am truly pierced with lances on every side, but always on the cross crying: long live Jesus! may his holy will be done in us! Patience amid so many sorrows.

  4. You were right to tell me that it must have been she, regarding your father's money.12 Well, God allowed it for our good.

  1. Tomorrow I will write at once; I will send you a teacher.

  2. Read these two lines to the little girls.

My little daughters, why upset yourselves so? Be good, for I will soon be with you, and whoever has been good will get a present; and let the nuns try to be good and keep the Rules; otherwise the holy Mother will know how to clean out her flock herself.13

Goodbye. The Lord bless you all, and you in particular.

Calling myself, as long as I live,

your very poor, but your own Mother Rosa

12. Write and tell me what debts you have, all of them, starting with the coarse flour;14 read this as best you can; it is one o'clock in the morning and I am still in poor health; I spent two days in bed.

1 The first remedy for her daughter's afflictions is a renewed act of abandonment to God's will. Advice and practical help follow, to relieve her at least partly in her responsibility for the community.

2 We are looking into: we are trying to find a priest here.

3 A priest's presence in the Institute ensured not only daily Mass; it also guaranteed the girls' moral and religious formation.

4 To keep the girls fit: better food, taking them out for walks (an «outing to the country»). She herself provides in part, sending provisions and money promptly.

5 She will not wait to be asked. Whenever she has money, she will share it with her.

6 Let us come to your sister. Her brief story as a Daughter of Saint Anne ends with her decision to leave the Institute for another place, presumably another Congregation, judging from M. Rosa's words to Francesca: it is certain that you do not want to change Institute.

7 How many lies! The Mother trenchantly sums up the underlying attitude and disloyal conduct of this creature, utterly contrary to the evangelical spirit of the Family of the holy Mother of Mary Immaculate.

8 What I did. Another summary: motherly love, trust given before and even after the betrayal, with a post of responsibility (as Superior of the Cento community), loving advice, a pedagogy of welcome, respect and appreciation (cf. Letters 113, 125, 126).

9 Now that she has withdrawn from the community and from her love, she entrusts her to the Lord, that he may have mercy on her and fill her with graces.

10 Be cheerful. Her joy lies in fidelity to two Mothers; her life will be nourished by their tenderness.

11 Now she demands all her trousseau and will not listen to reason. She takes no account of what the Institute spent on her, nor of what justice owes her sister, whose trousseau their mother had not completed in view of what the other daughter, who entered the Congregation first, had brought.

12 Evidently she had taken it for herself, excluding her sister.

13 A clear allusion to the cautionary event of those days: the departure from the Congregation of one of the first sisters to have taken the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

14 Farinotto: a kind of flour.

She informs him of an unpleasant incident caused by Fr. Angelo Ricchini. She has heard that the file on the dispute has passed into his hands and says she is comforted by this decision.

Most Reverend Excellency,

  1. Among the many persecutions with which the Very Rev. Fr. R. rages against our Institute, I take the liberty of pointing out to Your Excellency the latest, which seems to me harsher than the others.

  2. As to the one powerful father of the oppressed, I turn with complete confidence to Your Excellency's charity to be defended from the cruel persecution with which the Very Rev. Fr. Ricchini rages ever more fiercely against our Institute.

  3. Now, finding nothing else to seize on, he stirred up several women and sent them to the house to make a row demanding their girls; one of the girls refused, screaming, to go back to her family. Her mother threatened to abandon her; she bravely replied that she would have Saint Anne for her mother and would be glad never to see her again. The relatives had to leave, leaving the girl in the house of the Daughters of Saint Anne.2

  4. I have heard that the file which was in the Vicar's hands, that is, the little dispute between me and the Very Rev. Fr. R.,3 has been placed in Your Reverence's hands. How welcome this news was to me, since I have gained a new father and protector, and I am sure of a prompt welcome.4 From this incident,5 together with a host of others I dare not describe so as not to weary Your Excellency, you will understand how much we are persecuted.

  5. I hope Your Excellency will forgive me if I have written too familiarly, trusting to be protected by you, and assuring you that I have written with the greatest sorrow.

I await from Your Excellency your holy blessing, which will confirm your protection

your most humble Servant Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

2 Cf. Sr. A. Francesca Camisa's letter of 1 July 1869, which describes the incident in detail.

3 Very Rev. Fr. Ricchini.

4 Ricovero in the sense of welcome: I am sure of a prompt welcome.

5 From this incident, together with so many others I dare not describe,...

She suggests that she visit certain people to obtain help and advice for the work. News.

A.M.F.

Dear Francesca, my daughter,

  1. Go to Chiarella and to the Archbishop, if possible; but do this later, if you see that things are getting pressing, and all in agreement with the Superior.1 If you think the Superior would like a book of the Rules, give him one. Press for him or the other missionary to come and explain the Rules to you, or give you a little catechism.2

  2. Rest assured, I have written to Papa, to Chiarella and to Montano, and to the Bishop as well. You will see that the holy Mother will not fail to come to our aid.3

  3. Stand firm: do not hand over any girls without a note.4 My dear little daughter, I know well how you will suffer, and I assure you that the whole weight is on my shoulders; but courage, I have them here too,5 big and heavy ones. Patience!

  4. I told Papa everything; so if you could go to the canon and show your distress, but always with good manners and courtesy, begging him not to abandon us.6 I will write to him this evening, and you tell him so, saying that for charity's sake he should not abandon us, and that I would have come, but I left only two days ago and, being in poor health and not very well now, I cannot make the journey. Besides, the holy Mother's feast is approaching and we have many things to do.

  5. For the little exposition I will ask him again for the paper.7 If he knows anything of what they have granted, he will tell you how to proceed on point V, or 5; but before taking a step, consult the

Superior and write and tell me what he said. Go at once, but without saying anything; always take the one of the Good Shepherd,8 but silence, so that the Sisters do not hear. Write me everything calmly. Go to Fantini9 at once without asking anyone's advice; go at once, commend yourself to him, for charity's sake, always showing that you expect everything from him and want his advice. Do you understand?

  1. I am sorry about Bodda,10 but the Lord will want him with him; make yourself useful, and if he dies, all go to his funeral with the girls; and tell his mother to come and stay with you, and if she wants to come here, you will bring her with the little boy,11 or else alone, because, you know, the boy would be too much of a burden for us. I hope you received the telegram; the sack of maize flour is being held at the station.

  2. I received the biscuits and all the other things; thank you warmly for thinking of me and sending me the sweets. The Lord bless you; and if my prayers are acceptable to God, believe me, you will have a place in Paradise near the holy Mother; and if it pleases his Divine Majesty to forgive this infamous Mother of yours her sins and give her Paradise, we will be near each other.

Goodbye. Greet them all for me; I am

your most loving Mother in Saint Anne

1 She thinks it important for her to go to the Vicar Andrea Chiarella and to Archbishop Andrea Charvaz if things get worse, and in any case after consulting the Superior of the Lazarists, Father Francesco Dassano, who was responsible for the community's spiritual formation through instructions and conferences.

2 Or else catechism.

3 Rest assured. This advice to the Superior is extremely important, because the work itself is in danger because of Fr. Angelo Ricchini. For several months relations with him had soured. Instead of supporting and helping the work, he obstructed it by word and deed. Two days earlier the Superior had written to the Mother his very words of threat: «I will do everything to bring it all down». And deeds had followed: three mothers of resident girls had come to her to take their daughters away, first without and the next day with the note of authorisation from Fr. Ricchini that she had required. The same women had grossly insulted her in the street (cf. Sr. A. Francesca Camisa's letter of 1 July 1869).

Seeing the situation worsening, the Mother had hastened to write to her father and to the religious superiors: to the Vicar (not favourable to the Sisters, cf. Letter 131), to the Bishop, cf. Letter 134, and to Signor Niccolò Montano (cf. Letter 132, n. 7).

4 Stand firm: the Superior had kept to precisely this order: not to hand girls over to their mothers without Fr. Ricchini's written authorisation.

5 I have them: crosses.

6 Go to the Canon. Certainly Canon Melchiorre Fantini, also of the Archiepiscopal Curia of Genoa, who had been charged with settling the dispute. Cf. text, par. 5: «Go to Fantini at once...».

7 For the little exposition. She will ask again for authorisation to expose the Blessed Sacrament in the chapel for adoration; you will ask him (Fantini) how to proceed regarding point V of that authorisation.

8 The one of the Good Shepherd. The expression is unclear. Perhaps she meant: take with you as companion (as the Rules prescribed), as usual, Sr. A. of the Good Shepherd Bastia, the assistant superior.

So take them back, for every action we do against our own ill will, purely for love of him, will always please the Eternal; we see creatures and love them.

  2. As for the Reverend's letter:3 two badly written words on a sheet full of insults? Well, are you not glad4 that Jesus treats you this way, sending you these affronts in writing, since he sees you are still too weak to take them face to face, so that you can practise?

  3. What a dear Spouse! How well he knows how to treat5 his beloved ones, by what means he gracefully and gently trains them in perfection!
