She has been told that the Sisters speak loudly. She expresses regret at their failure to keep «mitigated» silence; she rebukes, advises and demands reparation.

A.M.F.

Our daughters,

  1. I felt a mortal wound1 when I was told that in that house people were talking so loudly that they could be heard even from the street.

  2. Dear holy Mother, what must it have been for your most sensitive heart, which was surely torn with grief at the sight of the offence your unworthy Daughters gave the Most High.2 Alas! From the questions I put to the people who heard them, those shouts were during the time of mitigated silence.3

  3. Truly,4 today, as I came back from the parlour at the end of recreation, my mind was quite distraught with the thought: what will become of those wretched creatures now that it is recreation time? Their racket will certainly have doubled.5

  4. And I imagined you afterwards at the nurses' class: surely, without considering that they can be heard on every side, they will shout as they used to here, far from other houses.

  5. My God! Truly, if I could have sent someone to you, if I myself could have, I would have flown there to prevent such a scandal.

  6. What can you plead before God the Father to excuse this fault? That you did not think of it, not being used to it? No, no, because this Mother of yours warned you a million times, first urging you to this observance, giving you examples, showing you the harm that comes from this great fault; and then, with regard to this new house, I added that you must be very careful and circumspect in speaking, moving and laughing, because you are among excellent

priests, whom you risk scandalising if you make a noise.

  1. Remember the Father's words and keep them constantly in mind, and the sorrow you always cause him when he sees that you never want to put into practice what he teaches you so fervently.

  2. So do penance for this fault of yours,6 to appease the Eternal Father, by keeping strict silence for two days; and for the whole week let your recreation be silent, and conduct your school entirely in mitigated silence. In this way you can partly make amends for the great wrong you have done.

God bless you, and I am

your poor Mother Rosa

Casa Dal Verme [Sampierdarena], 8 January 18707

1 A mortal wound. Talk so loud that it could be heard from the street had made a bad impression on a friend of the Institute, who felt bound to warn the Mother. She was deeply pained.

2 Mother Saint Anne could not but grieve at the conduct of her Daughters, who broke the Rules so openly and light-heartedly.

3 Mitigated silence. On this the Rules of 1869, ch. 9, 19 prescribed: «this silence is to be kept throughout the day (except during the time of strict silence and recreation)» and requires «that you do not speak without some need... and speak in a very low voice».

4 So strong was her impression — my mind was quite distraught — that she could not take her thoughts off the community at its various times of day.

5 In her corrective treatment, aimed at cutting out the evil at once and at the root, the Mother uses pejorative terms: wretched, that is, highly blameworthy; doubled racket, noisy, excited shouting. She is emotionally involved and brings all her natural and supernatural gifts to bear to save these thoughtless Daughters, recalling them on several points:

  • the offence given to God by a transgression they were aware of, having been taught by her over and over again, «millions of times!»;

  • the scandal given to others;

  • the sorrow caused to Father Tornatore.

6 So do penance. Finally she gives the remedy, reasoned and salutary, patiently taking her Daughters' weakness upon herself and presenting herself in her limitations: your poor Mother.

7 The date is at the end of the letter, wrongly preceded by the place-name Casa Dal Verme instead of Sampierdarena, where she was. This slip too has its meaning, revealing a state of mind.

She is at her parents' house, looking after her sick father. She asks for news and prayers.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of our Eternal Father be with you

my good daughter,

Blessed be our holy Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Today I received your letter giving me news of the will of the vice1 and of the communion.

  2. You tell me that Caterina is tiresome. Well, patience is needed; use punishment if they do not heed words.2

  3. Now I really want to know how they put Papa's name in the will. You know that Papa is Francesco, because if they had put Emanuele instead it would not be valid and there could be complications. Are you quite sure they said Francesco? Write and tell me.

  4. Now I am at Papa's house, because this evening at five my brother Francesco came with the carriage to fetch me, as Papa was unwell; so tonight I may sit up with him. At this moment the doctor and all the others are round the bed, so I am using these minutes to answer you, so as not to give rise3 to telegrams, which give me certain jolts that are not very pleasant.

  5. I would like to know whether you have done what I wrote to you in the first letter and whether you have received them all; this is the fourth.4 Poor me if I had four daughters like you! I would need a clerk just for them.5 You know well that I have all sorts of business; truly this poor head is crammed with a thousand affairs that take up no little of my mind.

  1. How is my health? I do not know.6 This morning I could

not even go and make the meditation with the others. Patience! If it pleases the Lord to humble this poor servant of his, so be it, for I receive everything gladly from his hands, blessing him a thousand times over when I feel the blow.7

  1. If, unfortunately, anything should go wrong with the looms and other things, write to me, and I will fly there; but I hope all will go well until I have finished everything here.

  2. I will not tell you about the ceremony, because I know those two, Sr. A. M. Vincenza and the Delegate, described it all to you yesterday.

  3. Tonight I am in purgatory, amid the tumult of the world,8 where nothing reigns but offence against God. Pray, for it is a time to pray and to act, working tirelessly for Jesus.9 I am going

to Papa.

I am your poor

Mother Rosa

10. God bless you and all the others. Pray, pray for this mother of yours who does not pray;10 make up for my sloth, so that I may not be lost in an eternity of pains. I am very tired.

Goodbye!

1 Will: the testator cannot be identified.

2 Caterina, one of the girls, sorely tries the educators' patience. The Mother repeats the educational norms of the time: patience first of all; firm measures, punishment, when words fail because they go unheeded.

3 Not to give rise. Not to give you cause for alarm that would lead you to send me telegrams. These were generally used for urgent or sad news, so receiving them made her anxious: certain jolts that are not very pleasant, as she says.

4 The four letters the Mother mentions are missing. Only two survive from this period, dated 7 and 8 January.

5 If I had four daughters like you, wanting a letter a day, I would need a clerk just for them. The tone is playful, not at all resentful.

6 My health... You ask how my health is? I do not know. She skips the details so as not to worry Adelaide.

7 On every occasion, happy or sad, she bears witness to loving adherence to God's will.

8 She feels painfully the difference of atmosphere between her religious family and her natural family.

9 Here is the corrective: the witness of a life ordered according to God's plan, prayer and charitable action.

10 Who does not pray. Staying with her family, she cannot keep a place and time for prayer. She counts this as her fault: my sloth.

She suggests following Fr. Tornatore's directions and urges living daily life realistically, looking at and imitating Jesus.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father, our all, be with us!

My beloved little daughter,

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Today I acknowledge receipt of your three letters; I am sure you will not hold it against me1 that I did not answer at once, being very busy.

  2. Tonight at last I am in our house, tired as a beast of burden.2

  3. You speak of taking postulants; I will not reply to that, because the Father is there and he will tell you how to proceed. When he sees them he will do what he thinks best. As for money, spend as the Father tells you.

  4. Tell the miller to send me three sacks of white flour. He still has 18, so send me three at once.

  5. Be calm, for the Lord will soon free me from this business and I will soon be with you.3

  6. I am waiting for the paper, because I must present it to the Curia, and now I cannot leave until I have settled this house's affairs and left these poor creatures calm and secure in every respect.

  7. Now, my daughter, for charity's sake, do not let yourself be seized by crotchets and vague ideas,4 all things that muddle the mind and serve only to disturb us and make us irritable. Let us keep to

what is positive, and let us try hard always to reason with the Crucifix before us, not at our side; let us look at him in all our actions, [to see] whether they conform to his pattern, and then everything is reduced to nothing and our sufferings become nothing at all, less than nothing.5

  1. Our daughter, where are your oh-so-cruel sufferings? I cannot find them, because when I look at my Jesus and then at his Bride Sr. A. M. Adelaide, I see nothing I could lay on the least of his wounds; I look for her suffering and cannot find even enough to relieve the least of Jesus' pains.6 Does our tooth ache? Well, they smashed all of Jesus' teeth and his mouth streamed with blood. Can you find no one to tell your sorrows and afflictions to? I see a Father who listens to you and comforts you, and this poor Mother of yours, who would give anything to make you truly crucified, so that one fine day you may die on Jesus' bed, and then, and then, in Paradise for eternity! There is no more cross there, no more suffering. Only love, love! And it is stocked with every sweet imaginable.7

  2. Cheer up! Cheer up! For Jesus likes those who suffer. Whoever does not want to suffer does not want to love...

Goodbye. Jesus in the heart, as on the lips. God bless you and all the others.

And I am your poor Mother Rosa

1 You will not count it a fault.

2 She had spent five days with her family looking after her sick father.

3 Be calm... I will soon be with you. A touch of human consolation, to help her get beyond her self-absorption and see and understand the difficulties of the sisters at Sampierdarena.

4 Crotchets and vague ideas. Mood swings and daydreams. Keep to reality, to what is concrete and positive.

5 Nothing, less than nothing. A strong conclusion to a teaching born of her experience of unitive love for «her crucified Good», the all of her nothing.

6 To relieve the least of Jesus' pains. This expression too evokes an intense life in Christ crucified, her mystical ardour, her cry to the Father: «Eternal Father, give me these pains and relieve my Good!» (M 2, p. 142). Yet in guiding her daughters along the mystical way she herself travelled, she knows how to adapt to their moral stature.

7 Cf. 2 Tim 2:11-12.

The importance of suffering, in fidelity to the Father's plan. How a superior should correct the sisters.

A.M.F.

Our daughter,

  1. You are right to complain of my silence, but fear for my health is what kept me from writing to you before. For many days I have been weaker than usual, and it weighs on me, making me give way3 on the bed. Tonight it is not so bad, but my stomach trouble makes up for it, and I assure you it keeps me excellent company.

  2. Let us bless the hand of the Almighty,4 which strikes us gently and charitably makes us pay our debts during this brief passage through a foreign land.

  3. My exile has already reached its thirty-eighth year, and with joy I can say [that] by the good fortune of having spent them always under the scourge of suffering, my only joy, my treasure.5

Yes, my daughter, only in suffering have I been able to find my delight, all my consolation, and it shortens my confinement in this painful prison.6

  1. Every new day, a new cross. Blessed is the one for whom dawn breaks among thorns and pains.7 Ah! that, you know, is truly the one marked by the finger of the Eternal Father; so, more than all others, we must revere him and, rejoicing with him, bless all his ways.8

  2. Our daughter, I fear I am boring you by speaking of nothing but suffering in this letter. But what can I do? When I begin to speak of it, I stop to think of it, I taste its sweetness, I lose myself in it and cannot get out again,9 because I never find I can have my fill. Ah! Blessed are the souls who can have their fill of it; they already taste

that divine nectar found only in the essence of suffering.

  1. As for the post of superior, or rather, as our holy Rules prescribe, Mother delegate:10 if she wishes, God gives her many means,11 looking at everything in God alone, in speaking and correcting, always with that holy peace; and truly let such correction be made only to please God, never letting the slightest feeling of our own have any part in it,12 but seeing only that the words that must come from us edify the sisters and serve to amend them, so that they feel them in their heart, and that the heart is so reproved that it has no other relief to calm its beating than to seek eagerly to amend.13

  2. The charity, gentleness and sweetness of the words of a mother correcting her daughters ensure that the sister's heart cannot help amending and becoming a true Daughter of Saint Anne.

  3. Try always to appear in the same mood, in prosperity and in adversity, always cheerful, because in adversity we have more reason to be content, since we know that by rejoicing in it we please our Lord. What greater consolation can we seek, when it pleases our Jesus?

  4. With the truth kept before our eyes,14 we cannot go astray on the Lord's path. Whoever acts with charity loves God greatly and neighbour as self, all by command of the Most High.

God bless you; pray, pray

and I am your poor Mother Rosa Gattorno

1 Not an autograph letter. It was copied out by the recipient and found among her papers.

2 The letter is dated 1871, but is presumed to be from 1870, for three internal reasons:

I. There is a remark by the Mother about her age. In January 1870 she had turned 38 just three months earlier, having been born on 14 October 1831.

II. Sr. A. Adelaide had been superior of the Piacenza community for almost four months (cf. Letter 151, 4).

III. In style and content the letter fits well among the others the Mother wrote to her at that time.

Fr. Fiocchi too had doubts about the dating, but relying only on one certain fact — the Mother's date of birth, which he calculated a year out — and not taking into account Sr. Adelaide's office as superior, he placed the letter two years earlier: 1869.

3 Making me give way. Confining me to bed.

4 The hand of the Almighty. She sees it at work in her life, as a fatherly

hand that, striking gently, tests our fidelity and, charitably, with loving finesse, purifies us during this brief passage through a foreign land.

5 My exile has reached its 38th year. Looking back on her life, she sees with joy God's personal plan for her, the vocation to suffer: a suffering that is my only joy, treasure, delight, consolation. It is a feeling shared by many saints.

Saint Paul had said: «I am filled with comfort; I am overjoyed in all our affliction» (2 Cor 7:4).

6 It shortens. Suffering shortens my time imprisoned in the body. Foretasting the joy of being in God and longing to possess him fully, she feels the mysterious groaning that makes her long for the soul's release from the painful prison of the body.

Here too the parallel with Saint Paul comes naturally: «We are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord» (2 Cor 5:8).

7 Blessed... happy is the one for whom dawn breaks each day amid tribulations and pains. Rosa embraces the summit of Jesus' teaching: whoever would follow him must take up his cross daily.

8 That is truly the one marked by the finger of the Eternal Father, the one the Eternal Father takes particular care of. So we, chosen and marked by him, must revere him above all and, rejoicing with him, bless all his ways and every choice he makes for us (cf. Eph 2:4-5).

9 The call to follow Jesus closely, sharing in the mystery of his passion, is a priceless gift. When she speaks or thinks of it she tastes its sweetness and loses herself in it, never satisfied. Ah! Blessed are the souls who can have their fill of it! Pain is the seed of glory. «Rejoice in so far as you share Christ's sufferings» (1 Pet 4:13).

10 The second part of the letter is a short but dense teaching for the Superior, then called Mother delegate, as representative of the Superior General and delegated by her to lead the community (Rule of 1869, ch. 7, 2).

11 If she wishes. If she is aware of it, God gives her many graces.

12 Truly let such correction. Correction should be made to please God, who «treats us as sons» — and what son is there whom his father does not discipline? (cf. Heb 12:7) — and our feelings must never have a part in it.

13 The words that come from us should «build up» and enliven the sisters, go down into their hearts and move them to sorrow, so that they feel no other need than to be freed through repentance.

14 The truth... (cf. Eph 4:15).

She asks to be met at the station.

A.M.F.

Our daughter for ever,

1. Just two lines to let you know that on Wednesday I will be at Piacenza station at noon, alone.1 I hope you will be there. Goodbye. God bless you.

I am your poor Mother

1 Wednesday, 26 January.

She reports on her journey and urges joy.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of our Eternal Father be with us

My Franceschina,

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Two hurried lines, so that they reach the post in time. By a miracle I am alive2 and, as you see, I am writing in my own hand; but I arrived utterly dead, and indeed I very nearly stayed in the railway carriage. Imagine: without a drop of coffee or water, I got here a few minutes after seven. Now let us leave everything in the hands of our Eternal Father, as I have already handed it over to him.3

  2. Come now, be cheerful, for your mother wants it! Yes, my daughter, comfort me with two lines telling me that you are as this poor Mother of yours wants: cheerful and always ready to receive his Cross from your Spouse's hands, to lighten his load a little.4 Yes, is that not so, my Franceschina?

  3. Answer me that you will embrace your Cross and give it a thousand kisses for me; I will say to Jesus: «give my little daughter the lighter part and the heavier part to me».

Goodbye. I am your poor Mother Sr. A. M. Rosa

4. P.S. God bless you together with the others, whom I hope soon to hear are truly the Daughters of Saint Anne and my dear jew-

els, whom I hold close to my breast for eternity, all with me. Tell Blandina to revive her faith5 and pray for me.

1 Given the date of her return to Piacenza, 26 January, this letter is from the following day.

2 By a miracle I am alive. The Mother suffered greatly when travelling and must have been taken ill. Things were made worse by the train's considerable delay; it should have arrived at noon, as she had said in her previous letter.

3 Even from this experience of the cross she draws an ascetical lesson.

4 Cheerful... cheerful, always ready to receive the cross from the Spouse's hands. This is one of the most striking features of the Daughter of Saint Anne as it emerges from the Foundress's letters.

5 Sr. A. Blandina was ill.

She urges silence and the keeping of the holy Rules in every part, from the smallest to the greatest prescriptions.

A.M.F.

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate Our daughter for ever,

  1. I have received your letters; be calm and pray a great deal, slowly and fervently. It will be a good thing if you put silence into practice, the one good for a Religious and a sure means of acquiring all the other virtues; remember that one easily falls into idle words, and often they are conversations forbidden by our holy Rules.2

  2. Daughter, that holy little book our Father T.3 gave us, after writing it at heaven's dictation, we wretches take so little notice of it. Reflect, daughter, that these are the word of God, and if we want to become holy we must put them into practice; begin with the smallest, and these will open the way for us to keep the great ones.

  3. How beautiful it will be when one day this little book is what earns us a most beautiful crown of Glory!

I will add nothing more, because I do not feel very well

I am your poor Mother Rosa. Tell Sr. A. Francesca that I will write to her at length tomorrow...

1 This date is almost certain, given the context of the correspondence.

2 The Rules of 1869 had been printed in pocket format.

3 Giovanni Battista Tornatore.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of our Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Blessed daughter and my superior, and Vincenza, and both of you

  1. Cheer up, for in a few days I will be with you again. For charity's sake, if any summons1 should come, accept it, keep it with you and write to me at once. If I am not there yet, you, my Vincenza, go at once to your uncle and try to get [a] petition drawn up, and then take it. Go together, the two of you, with Signora Morando.2 She has courage and is good in these situations; being a lay person she can say rather more than you, who must have great regard for your habit, with one foot in Paradise and the other in the world, to drag the cross along.

  2. Take the summons to Papa, if it comes. If you need anything, write and tell me.

Goodbye. Greet Carlotta for me.

3. I enclose a letter to take to the Mayor's wife. Read it and leave it open. You too beg her to accept this office.3 I have already written to many other ladies;4 I hope I can manage everything. In a moment I am writing to Fr. Luigi and sending him another thirty books, with a dozen bottles of wine. And the same to Fr. Accinelli.5 Let Sr. A. Blessed be our glorious Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

May the blessing of our Eternal Father be with us

My beloved daughter,

  1. Two more lines, so that this time you cannot complain that I do not write. Listen: the red cotton I brought you2 with the white, have it twisted two-ply, [one] white and one red, and make something with it in crochet.

My Mamma

  1. I am answering your letter, which I received only a few hours ago. I hear how kind Giusta1 was to go and visit Carlottina; thank her and tell her to remember our poor chapel.

  2. I cannot describe the pleasure I felt on hearing that at last Papa is gladly embracing everyone and clearing away the rust; what a grace! Tell me, Mamma, how great is your consolation? It cannot be described. I can imagine it.2

[ ]

(a few lines follow from the superior Adelaide, who concludes the letter)6

The Foundress's mother.

May the blessing of our Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter,

Blessed be our holy Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My Vincenza, all mine,

  2. For several days I have been in two minds, and now I have decided to write to the Father Superior, to have from his holy lips a ruling on the point I am now writing to you about.2

Listen, the case is this3 — which, unfortunately, still occurs among us. Suppose I were in church while the Priest was giving Holy Communion, and I were asked something — say by the nurse, because a sister had been taken ill, or because a sister wanted to get up and come to church — and I had to answer with just two words. Is it right, first of all, for me to let the nurse talk at such length? And then to answer? I say: our Rules say that not a single word may be spoken. That would be enough to make me leave at once; and then there is the irreverence to God, who at that moment is in the priest's hands.

trouble. My opinion, on the contrary, is first of all not to let her speak; secondly, even if I had to do so after communion, always to go out, or else to go back in and go straight to the altar; for even if that disturbance had distracted me, Jesus, who so loves such respect and veneration in his temple, would come to me and give me greater recollection than I would have had if I had stayed to answer in church.

  1.   1. Already half the month of the Sacred Heart of Jesus has gone. I had meant to write to you at the very beginning1 of this month, but partly my health and partly my heavy duties have made me put off writing to you until today.

  2. Now I will dip my pen2 in this fluid of the most divine Heart of Jesus, his most holy Blood, so as to deal properly with certain points of the holy Rules that I found neglected.

  3. First. Mitigated silence.3 Daughters, truly I tell you that these words of yours4 are so many wounds to the heart of your holy Mother Saint Anne. That unrestrained laughter during recreation! Remember that you are religious, brides of a Spouse who is all courtesy and grace and does not like coarseness.

  4. Now I leave it to you to make a careful examination and then to pray the Sacred Heart to open the cleft of his Side5 and, in his mercy, keep you inside, so that in that Sacred Heart you may learn most sublime lessons.

  5. Remember the day of holy Retreat, and make it entirely for my intention. I will stop, because it is too late.

In the Sacred Heart I clasp you all and call myself

Your poor Mother 439

1 At the beginning of this month.

2 I will dip my pen in the blood of Jesus' most divine heart, to give my words the power to enlighten you on the points of the Rules I found you were not keeping.

3 Mitigated silence, cf. Letter 178.

4 These words of yours. Trivial, useless words, since during mitigated silence speech was allowed only «out of necessity» or about «holy and edifying things» (Rules of 1869, ch. 10, 19).

5 Open the cleft of his Side. For Mother Rosa, as for countless other mystics, the most holy Humanity of Christ is the gateway to unitive encounter. She offers her daughters her own way of love, so that they may learn most sublime lessons, the only truly transforming ones.

She urges trust in God and confidence in Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our holy Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter,

  1. A hurried line, because I have not a moment. Do not worry,1 my health is the same as ever, but since I have been here I have not yet had to stay in bed.

  2. Thank you for your concern for this unworthy Mother of yours. May God reward your care.

  3. I am sorry you have not yet been able to pay any of the bills; well, the holy Mother will pay them all, do not doubt it. Trust in God and you will have everything.2

  4. Be cheerful with Jesus.3 Yes, my daughter: when we have the Eternal God with us, what more do we lack? Nothing! We are truly rich, rich, and we challenge the whole world, because it is all ours, since it belongs to our Spouse.4

Goodbye. I will be with you soon.

Poor Mother Rosa

1 Do not worry.

2 Whoever has faith obtains everything (cf. Mk 11:24).

3 Be cheerful. Faith expressed in gospel joy, with simple, complete trust in providence (cf. Mt 6:25-34).

4 We are truly rich, rich. The beatitude of poverty, lived in the spirit of Saint Francis of Assisi, the Father Rosa had followed on the way of poverty as a tertiary.

She expresses her own and the community's regret that the coming feast of Saint Anne will not be gladdened and comforted by his fatherly presence.

Most Reverend Excellency,

  1. The feast of the commemoration of Saint Anne is approaching, the day on which in past years Your Excellency1 used to come and bring your Blessing to this Community of yours, which was born and is growing under your fatherly direction.

  2. Allow me, O Good Shepherd, to express my sorrow at so great a privation. Truly, it is no longer the day we longed for; none of the preparations holds our attention as we make them, because everything brings us sadness and pain. I can swear to you that our arms seem not to know how to move to decorate the Chapel.

  3. Send us at least your fatherly blessing, then, and it will comfort and relieve us poor creatures after a year of anguish. On that day every sorrow lessened and gave us strength to undertake a new year of greater sacrifices.

  4. Nothing else can relieve me of so many sorrows but to receive your fatherly blessing, which2 I, with my forehead to the ground, and all of us prostrate at your feet, await, as I sign myself with the deepest esteem and veneration Your Excellency's

most humble Sr. A. M. Rosa Gattorno

1 The feast of the commemoration of Saint Anne is approaching, on which Your Excellency...

2 Which.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My blessed daughter,

  1. Just one line, because you know I am so busy that truly I have not a moment to breathe. I am constantly anxious about poor Sr. Crocifissa.1

  2. I would like to write to good Fr. Luigi, but I cannot. I will write to him this evening.

  3. As for your illness, it is not true that you cannot get better.2 And even if a remnant3 of illness were left, that would only mean you must always be on your guard so that it does not get worse; so I order you again4 to take every possible care and always eat animal fat, never oil. Giulia5 has the same illness and she too cannot take oil.

  4. I would like a letter every moment,6 so as to be kept constantly informed of Sr. Crocifissa's health.

Goodbye. I will write to you this evening.

I am your poor Mother

God bless you together with the others. Maria,7 who is here, sends you a thousand greetings.

1 Sr. A. Crocifissa Dugoni.

2 Francesca now thought the various treatments useless — the baths, the cure in Piacenza only recently finished — and was discouraged.

3 Remnant: a residue of the illness (chronic tracheitis).

4 I order you: I oblige you. The sisters tended to neglect themselves.

5 Perhaps Giulia Calieri, a friend of hers.

6 Every moment. Her motherly anxiety is truly great. Sr. A. Crocifissa died that same day at noon. Cf. the two letters of Fr. Luigi Decavi of 30 July 1870, Arch St FSA, G. 3. 27/5.

7 Maria d'Annenkoff.

She cannot answer the many long letters from the sisters in Piacenza. The value of correction.

A.M.F.

May the blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our blessed daughter,

  1. A few hours ago I received a letter from you together with others. My God! First of all, please read these two lines to the daughters there.

  2. My blessed daughters, I am not answering any of you, because I have not time even to read the letters1 you send me, since my health no longer allows me to stay up all night at my desk reading the very long things you write to me; for often I have to use even the time for prayers and meals.

  3. Besides, you have there the best you could wish for, our Father,2 for both temporal and spiritual matters. So it is pointless to write to me. Still less at such length.

  4. Your news is very dear to me; a little note inside one of your Delegate's letters I can read quickly and I welcome it; but some very long letters, to my regret, I have to set aside.

  5. I write this so that you know that if there is something in them, I cannot answer you. You must tell everything to the Father, and certainly you will find in him what this wretched creature can never give you or advise you so rightly.3

6. Your Mother delegate keeps me informed of your health, and every time I answer her I always implore heaven's blessing on you all.4

Goodbye... God bless you all and make you true Daughters of Saint Anne, intent only on putting her holy Rules into practice.5

  1. And you, my blessed daughter, who cannot bear so gentle6 a nip to your self-love? Ah! Would that this ugly monster7 were not only bitten but wholly devoured in Lucifer's belly, ugly monster that has nothing to do with the Daughters of Saint Anne.

  2. Well then, tell me: what do you find in those exhortations?8 Nothing; only listen: if, when we are corrected, the fault exists in us, the good is that we correct it; and if we do not have it, it will serve us first to gain merit before God, and then to correct others who may need it. The first is fine and noble,9 because by it we give glory and pleasure to God.

  3. Daughter, what a word: to give pleasure to God! Courage, for after rain comes fine weather. A slap taken for love of Jesus is a sweet.

  1. Listen, my daughter: whenever you do not want these sweets, send them to me and I will enjoy them with great pleasure, and I will say to the dear Eternal Father: give my beloved many other consolations, spiritual and temporal. That is the bargain. Are you happy?

  2. Be cheerful in carrying the cross;10 then you will not feel its weight so much. My occupations are immense and do not allow me to stay longer, because they are waiting for me in the parlour.

Goodbye. I am your most affectionate

M. Rosa

1 The sisters at the Mother House were now many, and as Father Tornatore was there to look after them spiritually and materially, the Mother felt they should not write her such long letters, which she had no time even to read, let alone answer.

2 Our Father. Note her affectionate deference and complete trust in him and his work.

3 If you have written something urgent, I cannot answer. The Father is there. Compared with the Father, a learned, wise, balanced man, wholly God's, she feels poor and ignorant, incapable of such right advice.

4 I implore heaven's blessing... God bless you. She begs the Father, giver of every good, to pour out his saving power on those daughters and act in their lives, making them true Daughters of Saint Anne, reaching only for holiness.

5 Her holy Rules. Hers, that is, Saint Anne's, the Mother who guides and points the way to perfect love.

6 So gentle, slight.

7 The Mother pours into her words all her indignation and loathing for self-love, which she considers the root of all evil.

8 Father Tornatore's exhortations.

9 The first. The first case: being corrected unjustly.

10 Cheerful in carrying the cross. Being full of joy in suffering is a clear element of Mother Rosa's spirituality.
